newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain denies torture in ETA suspect interrogation.
newsitem.headline: Spain denies torture in ETA suspect interrogation.

text.p: Basque nationalist leaders on Friday accused police of torturing a suspected ETA assassin, but authorities insisted his grave injuries were caused during a violent arrest.
Fernando Elejalde was taken to hospital from police cells semi-conscious and in serious condition on Thursday, two days after being captured by police.
"We are clearly looking at a case of abuse and the practice of torture," Basque Nationalist Party spokesman Joseba Egibar told journalists. "He was beaten within an inch of his life."

A hospital in the Basque city of San Sebastian said Elejalde was admitted with four crushed vertebrae in his lower back, internal bleeding from a ruptured kidney, a perforated eardrum, and bruises covering his face and body.

Spain's Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja called for an immediate investigation into the events and pleaded for calm in the troubled northern region where ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) guerrillas are fighting for independence.

He said on Friday that Elejalde, accused of shooting dead a prison psychologist in a presumed ETA attack on Tuesday, was badly hurt in an ensuing gunbattle with police on the streets of San Sebastian in which two police were also wounded. A second guerrilla, a woman, escaped.

Elejalde was taken to an emergency clinic which recorded his injuries as "coinciding substantially" with those reported two days later, proving he was hurt during arrest and not by torture, the minister said.

"This does not jibe with the scenario that he had been badly treated while held in the police department," Mayor Oreja said, adding that the suspect had confessed to having been hit by a car while fleeing.
But the minister, whose Popular Party (PP) government has vowed to follow the letter of the law in its fight against ETA, said the matter was still being treated as a possible case of police abuse.

"In this area no one can afford to retreat," he said. "Too many things have gone on in the past for us to be anything but completely uncompromising at times like these with what could be non-compliance with the law, if that is what has happened."
Mayor Oreja said he would appear before parliament on Monday to explain what happened to Elejalde.

In parliament earlier this week he had to explain what happened to another suspected ETA member who was found hanged in his prison cell with his feet and hands tied, facts that were not immediately released by the government.
Officials said it was a suicide, but Basque nationalists accused the government of a cover up and said it was "difficult to imagine" someone could hang themselves while bound.

The PP came to power last May after 13 years of Socialist rule, largely because of accusations the Socialist government ran a "dirty war" against ETA in the 1980s, using illegal methods like torture and kidnapping to combat the rebels.
The new conservative government has therefore been eager to present a clean-hands approach to fighting the rebels, who have killed some 800 people since 1968.

But fears still linger in the Basque region that the government could reinstate repressive measures imposed against Basques under the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco, which led to the rise of ETA.
Basque politicians say the government's harder line and the alleged police abuse will only serve to fuel ETA, which has stepped up its violence since the start of the year, killing seven people.
